raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the survival benefit of ICD therapy while avoiding chronic transvenous endovascular leads, historically the “weak link” of ICD systems. Randomized trials established ICDs for secondary prevention and for selected patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction [1–3], but long-term lead fracture, venous occlusion, endocarditis, extraction risk, and lead-related reintervention motivated a fully extrathoracic alternative.

The contemporary S-ICD consists of a lateral thoracic pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode that senses a far-field electrogram and delivers high-energy shocks. It does not provide chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP). Thus, the ideal candidate has a guideline-supported ICD indication, passes preimplant electrocardiographic screening, and has no current or anticipated need for pacing. Early human experience demonstrated reliable defibrillation but also highlighted higher defibrillation thresholds and sensing challenges compared with transvenous systems [4,5]. The pivotal IDE study confirmed safety and efficacy in 314 patients, with high induced ventricular fibrillation conversion success and acceptable short-term complication rates [6]. The EFFORTLESS registry, pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS analyses, and later 5-year data reinforced durable shock efficacy, low electrode failure, and a complication profile dominated by pocket-related issues and inappropriate shocks rather than intravascular lead failure [7–10]. The U.S. post-approval program extended these observations to a broader real-world cohort, including more comorbidity and operator heterogeneity, with preserved 5-year shock efficacy and very low electrode-related complication rates [11,12].

Programming and sensing have been central to S-ICD maturation. Early inappropriate shocks were frequently due to T-wave oversensing, supraventricular tachycardia, myopotentials, or low-amplitude R waves. Dual-zone programming with a conditional discrimination zone reduced inappropriate shocks without apparent loss of efficacy [14]. Meta-analytic data suggested that inappropriate shock rates with S-ICD and single-chamber transvenous ICDs were broadly comparable in earlier eras [15]. The UNTOUCHED trial, enrolling primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction and mandated contemporary programming, reported low inappropriate-shock rates, supporting high-rate cutoffs, discrimination, and modern filtering as key determinants of performance [13].

Randomized comparative evidence is now substantial. PRAETORIAN randomized patients with an ICD indication but no pacing indication to S-ICD or transvenous ICD and demonstrated noninferiority for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [16,17]. Important tradeoffs emerged: S-ICD patients had fewer lead-related complications, whereas transvenous ICD recipients benefited from ATP and atrial/near-field sensing. A PRAETORIAN therapy analysis showed that ATP reduced some appropriate shocks in transvenous systems, but overall arrhythmic efficacy remained acceptable in both groups [18]. A complication analysis showed different complication phenotypes, with systemic infections and lead dysfunction concentrated in transvenous ICD recipients and pocket hematoma or local issues more typical after S-ICD implantation [19]. ATLAS, focused on patients at elevated risk for lead complications, further supported fewer early serious lead-related perioperative events with S-ICD therapy [20]. Meta-analyses of randomized and propensity-matched studies generally show similar mortality and appropriate shock outcomes, fewer lead-related complications with S-ICD, and nuanced differences in inappropriate shock mechanisms [21,22].

Patient selection remains the clinical fulcrum. The S-ICD is attractive for younger patients, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, difficult venous access, prior device infection, dialysis, congenital heart disease, or high expected lifetime lead burden. Experience in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy supports feasibility, but dynamic electrocardiographic changes, exercise-related T-wave oversensing, and the possibility of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia requiring ATP require careful evaluation [23,24]. In Brugada syndrome, S-ICD avoids transvenous lead complications in young patients but may be vulnerable to sensing changes; registry data are therefore valuable for refining selection and programming [25,26].

Implant technique has also evolved. Intermuscular generator placement, two-incision techniques, careful parasternal lead positioning, and radiographic assessment have improved comfort, cosmesis, and defibrillation success. The PRAETORIAN score provides a structured radiographic method to predict defibrillation success after implantation [27]. PRAETORIAN-DFT suggests that score-guided omission of defibrillation testing may be safe in appropriately positioned systems, potentially reducing procedural risk [28]. Current European and U.S. guidelines recognize S-ICD as an alternative to transvenous ICD in patients who do not require pacing, particularly when venous access or infection risk is a concern [29,30]. Future directions include modular systems pairing S-ICD with leadless pacing to add bradycardia support and ATP without transvenous leads. For now, the S-ICD is best viewed not as a universal replacement but as a mature, evidence-based option whose advantages are greatest when lifelong lead avoidance outweighs the need for pacing therapies.
